clue.text: Wherein, in so many words, lawyers may feel at home

definitions.meaning: the clue words picture a well-known British dictionary, a book full of words, named after its publisher
barristers work from sets of rooms in the Inns of Court, their professional offices

explanation.surface: A riddle about where lawyers might feel comfortable, phrased in a roundabout legal way.
explanation.walkthrough: One sense is the Chambers Dictionary, a standard British reference book; the other is a barrister's chambers, the offices lawyers share.
explanation.definitionFit: Both the dictionary's publishing name and the barristers' offices share this one name, so the word suits both pictures.

clue.text: Circumscribe part of the theatre

definitions.meaning: to circumscribe is to draw a ring round something
the dress ... or upper ... is a tier of seats in a theatre

explanation.surface: A directive to mark off a section of a playhouse.
explanation.definitionFit: Drawing a ring round is a verb sense; a curved balcony tier of seating is the noun sense.

clue.text: A f-fruit? Come out with it!

parts.note: the hyphenated stammer models the fruit's name said with a stutter on its first letter, so a pear becomes p-pear

explanation.surface: Someone stammering over the name of a fruit is urged to spit the word out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'f-fruit' is a stuttered 'fruit', telling you to stutter the fruit you choose: P-PEAR. 'with it' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: To come out, as an actor onto a stage or a star in the sky, is to show up or become visible.

clue.text: Underwritten in reverse?

definitions.meaning: financially guaranteed or supported, as a sponsor supports a venture
moved backwards, as a driver reverses a car into a space

explanation.surface: A question whether an insurance guarantee could work backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Supported with money is one sense; having driven a vehicle backwards is the other.

clue.text: How Naomi could have reacted on losing her daughter-in-law

definitions.text: How Naomi could have reacted on losing her daughter-in-law

parts.words: How Naomi could have reacted on losing her daughter-in-law
parts.note: in the Bible, Naomi's daughter-in-law is Ruth; being left without Ruth would make Naomi Ruth-less, a pun on a word for pitilessly

explanation.surface: A question about the Biblical Naomi's feelings were she bereft of her loyal daughter-in-law.
explanation.walkthrough: In the Book of Ruth, Ruth refuses to leave her mother-in-law Naomi. Without her, Naomi would act 'Ruth-less-ly', which is also the adverb meaning without mercy.
explanation.definitionFit: The adverb means pitilessly or cruelly, but split up it says lacking Ruth, the Biblical daughter-in-law.

clue.text: Sweet little thing

definitions.meaning: a British dessert of sponge, fruit, custard and cream; sweet is British for pudding
a trivial matter or small amount

explanation.surface: A fond description of something small and charming.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain 'sweet' is the dessert course; this layered pudding is a classic one.
explanation.definitionFit: A layered custard pudding is one sense; a matter of no importance is the other.

clue.text: The country's changed, so I heard

indicators.note: the letters of the following words are altered into a new order

explanation.surface: Rumour has it that a certain nation has been transformed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'changed' rearranges SOIHEARD. The surface also nods to the fact that this country did change, becoming Zimbabwe.
explanation.definitionFit: The former name of the southern African state now called Zimbabwe.

clue.text: Fertiliser on the menu?

parts.note: a ground-up fish product spread on fields, read jokingly as a course of seafood offered in a restaurant

explanation.surface: A diner suspicious that the restaurant is serving garden fertiliser.
explanation.walkthrough: The product is ground dried fish used as fertiliser; split in two it reads as a dinner of fish.
explanation.definitionFit: Ground dried fish used to feed soil, which read as two words would be a seafood dinner.

clue.text: Stretcher for a one-time nurse

parts.note: former, abbreviated as the prefix ex
one who tends the sick, a tender

explanation.surface: A medical stretcher kept for a nurse who used to work there.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stretcher' suggests a hospital, but it means something that lengthens; 'for a' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that lengthens or prolongs a thing, as a table leaf lengthens a table.

clue.text: Greed for which a large town takes the blame at first

indicators.note: says the blame piece comes before the other pieces of the build

parts.note: to take the rap is to take the blame
a city is a large town

explanation.surface: A city gets blamed for avarice before anyone else.
explanation.walkthrough: 'takes the blame' points to the idiom 'take the rap'; 'at first' puts that piece ahead of the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: Grasping avarice; a predatory hunger for gain.

clue.text: Pet firms in a fix

parts.note: COS is the abbreviation for companies, which are firms
to set something is to fix it in place

explanation.surface: Companies find themselves in difficulty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in a fix' looks like trouble, but 'fix' is a verb synonym for SET; 'in a' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: To pet is to pamper or indulge, treating someone fondly.

clue.text: Where everybody recalls little Helen in Wales

indicators.note: calls back, so the word for everybody is read from its end to its start

parts.note: all means everybody

indicators.note: made short, so the pet name loses its final letter

parts.note: Nellie is a pet form of Helen

explanation.surface: A Welsh place where everyone remembers a small girl called Helen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'recalls' turns ALL to LLA; 'little' cuts NELLIE to NELLI. 'in Wales' completes the definition by locating the place.
explanation.definitionFit: A town on the south coast of Wales, so it answers the question of a place.

clue.text: An English composer, nevertheless

parts.note: Sir Edward, an English writer of light operas, bore a surname that is also the adjective for a nationality other than English

explanation.surface: Insisting that someone is English in spite of appearances.
explanation.walkthrough: Edward German (1862-1936) was an English composer; his surname names a different nationality, hence 'nevertheless'.
explanation.definitionFit: The surname of English composer Sir Edward, which also means coming from the country with Berlin as capital.

clue.text: Useful outlet when things get out of hand at house-warmings

definitions.text: Useful outlet when things get out of hand at house-warmings

parts.words: Useful outlet when things get out of hand at house-warmings
parts.note: a house-warming here is a building literally on fire, and the outlet is an emergency exit for leaving it

explanation.surface: A party tip about slipping away when a new-home celebration gets rowdy.
explanation.walkthrough: A house-warming is a party for a new home, but here it is a building literally heating up in a blaze.
explanation.definitionFit: An emergency staircase on the outside of a building, used to flee a blaze.

clue.text: Absorb recooked meal as it is

indicators.note: cooked again, so the letters of the words that follow are reworked

explanation.surface: A cook reheats a dish and eats it without changing it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'recooked' rearranges MEALASITIS.
explanation.definitionFit: To take in and incorporate, as the body takes in food.

clue.text: Vessel in which the crew can hold their liquor

definitions.text: Vessel in which the crew can hold their liquor

parts.words: Vessel in which the crew can hold their liquor
parts.note: a vessel is both a ship and a drinking glass, and holding liquor is both carrying it and staying sober

explanation.surface: A ship whose sailors cope well with heavy drinking.
explanation.walkthrough: The word names a two-masted sailing ship and also a large glass for sherry or beer.
explanation.definitionFit: A fore-and-aft rigged sailing ship and also a tall drinking glass.

clue.text: Refreshing drink, but another is a different matter

definitions.meaning: a serving of the hot beverage brewed from leaves
the idiom 'another ... altogether' describes something quite different

explanation.surface: Accepting a reviving drink, but declining a second one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Quite another cup of tea' is a British idiom for an entirely different matter.
explanation.definitionFit: A brewed hot drink, and in idiom with 'another' something of a different kind.

clue.text: Retinues badly in need of food

indicators.note: poorly arranged, so the letters of the word before are jumbled

explanation.surface: A royal entourage left badly short of provisions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'badly' rearranges RETINUES.
explanation.definitionFit: A literary adjective for hungry or greedy.

clue.text: Took advice from Dulles once

indicators.note: the letters come from the words that follow and are made into something new

explanation.surface: Someone took guidance from the American statesman Dulles in times past.
explanation.walkthrough: 'from' is a light anagram signal, rearranging DULLESONCE. John Foster Dulles was a US Secretary of State; 'once' looks like the time, but it is fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: In its older sense the verb means took counsel, consulted others for advice.

clue.text: Held forth on exemption from VAT…

definitions.meaning: spoke at length, made a speech
goods free of British sales tax are zero-rated

explanation.surface: Someone lectured at length on tax-exempt goods.
explanation.walkthrough: VAT is the UK's value added tax. Goods exempt from it are 'zero-rated', written here as O-RATED with O for zero. 'on' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: To speak pompously at length is one sense; tax-free at a nought rate, written with O, is the other.

clue.text: … the thing to present an argument against

definitions.meaning: to raise a protest or opposition

explanation.surface: Continuing the previous clue: the item one argues against.
explanation.definitionFit: A noun meaning item, and a verb meaning to protest, sharing one spelling.

clue.text: Russian port using some poetry as uplift?

parts.note: odes are poems, some poetry

indicators.note: in a down clue, lifted up means read from bottom to top

explanation.surface: Poetry used to raise the spirits in a seaport.
explanation.walkthrough: 'uplift' turns AS upwards to SA in this down entry; 'using' is a link. The port, now in Ukraine, was in the Russian Empire and the USSR.
explanation.definitionFit: A Black Sea port, long part of the Russian Empire and Soviet Union.

clue.text: Sullen in large measure, but they smell nice

indicators.note: the gloomy word goes inside the size abbreviation

parts.note: OS is outsize, a large clothing measure
dour means sullen and gloomy

explanation.surface: A grumpy person surrounded by pleasant scents.
explanation.walkthrough: Outsize is a British clothing size for large garments. 'in' is the container signal; 'but' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Smells or scents; the clue picks the pleasant kind, though the word covers any smell.

clue.text: Attributed to a man of letters in modern times

indicators.note: the writer word is placed within the era abbreviation

parts.note: AD, anno Domini, marks the current era
a scribe is a writer or copyist

explanation.surface: Work credited to a literary figure of the present day.
explanation.walkthrough: 'man of letters' suggests an author, but means a copyist. 'in' is the container signal and 'to a' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Credited to a source or regarded as caused by something.

clue.text: Crazy type from Br

annotationWithheld.why: Clue held as 'Crazy type from Br (6)': cut short after 'Br', so the wordplay cannot be read; no scan and no search found the rest.

clue.text: One to whom orders may be sweet

definitions.text: One to whom orders may be sweet

parts.words: One to whom orders may be sweet
parts.note: a diner's order may be for a dessert course, and the server takes it

explanation.surface: Someone who enjoys being told what to do.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sweet' is British for dessert: the order is for a pudding, not pleasant to receive.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman who serves at table in a restaurant and takes diners' orders.

clue.text: Specialities at Astor's Carvery

indicators.note: a place where meat is carved up, so the letters of the name before are cut and rearranged

explanation.surface: The signature dishes at a carving restaurant owned by Astor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Carvery' signals an anagram by carving up ASTORS. A carvery is a British restaurant serving joints of meat sliced to order.
explanation.definitionFit: Joints of meat cooked in the oven, the signature dishes of a carving restaurant.

clue.text: Prolonged quarrel that can be bloody

definitions.text: Prolonged quarrel that can be bloody

parts.words: Prolonged quarrel that can be bloody
parts.note: a long feud between families, often fought with killing and revenge

explanation.surface: A long-running dispute that may turn violent or merely annoying.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bloody' could be a British mild swearword, but here it is literal: blood feuds.
explanation.definitionFit: A long-running blood feud, especially between families seeking revenge.
